item.title: Why CIOs must prepare for hybrid quantum computing
item.description:
For IT leaders mapping out the next five to ten years of computational strategy, the true business value of quantum will not be unlocked by independent quantum processors operating in a vacuum. Instead, the future lies in the seamless orchestration of hybrid cyberinfrastructure—where quantum processing units (QPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), and classical high-performance computing (HPC) environments operate in tandem.

This paradigm shift is exactly what is driving the latest strategic investments at the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center (PSC).

Moving beyond standalone quantum systems

For years, the narrative surrounding quantum computing has focused heavily on the hardware timeline: counting qubits, minimizing error rates, and anticipating the arrival of fault-tolerant systems. While those milestones remain critical, Dr. Bruno Abreu, the Director of Research & Development at PSC, highlights a more immediate operational challenge: integration.

Enter TangleLab, a groundbreaking hybrid quantum-classical supercomputing platform led by the PSC. Backed by a $5 million grant from the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) and built in partnership with HPE and Rigetti Computing, TangleLab serves as a national testbed. Its core goal is to understand how QPUs can be tightly integrated with classical HPC systems to manage complex, multi-tiered workflows.

“We are not deploying a standalone quantum computer,” Abreu notes. “Our goal is to make TangleLab the prototype open platform for a future where quantum information processing and distribution are core elements of advanced cyberinfrastructure.”

For CIOs, this strategy underscores a vital truth: quantum will not replace your classical infrastructure. Instead, it will act as a highly specialized accelerator. Just as GPUs revolutionized machine learning workloads by taking over parallel processing tasks from CPUs, QPUs will step in to handle highly specific, mathematically complex sub-problems that classical binary logic struggles to solve.

Defining “quantum utility” for the enterprise

A key theme of a This Week in HPC interview is the shift from pursuing abstract “quantum supremacy” to achieving practical “quantum utility.” In an enterprise context, quantum utility occurs when a hybrid system delivers an optimized solution—whether measured by speed, accuracy, cost, or energy efficiency—that classical infrastructure cannot achieve alone.

By pairing Rigetti quantum hardware with HPE advanced supercomputing architectures and classical GPUs, TangleLab is designed to tackle specialized optimization and simulation problems. The target application areas have direct corollaries in the commercial sector:

  • Advanced chemistry and materials science: Accelerating molecular modeling for pharmaceuticals, energy storage, and manufacturing.
  • Complex optimization tasks: Solving multi-variable logistical, supply chain, and financial risk problems.
  • Cryptography and security: Preparing enterprise data architecture for the post-quantum encryption landscape.

By investigating these hybrid quantum-classical workflows today, PSC is laying the software and algorithmic groundwork required to make quantum resources composable and scalable for real-world scientific and industrial applications.

Cultivating a quantum-ready workforce

Beyond the technical hurdles of hardware and software integration, Dr. Abreu highlights a critical bottleneck that every CIO must confront: the talent gap. Developing applications for a hybrid supercomputing environment requires an entirely new blend of skills. Engineers must understand classical HPC optimization, AI/ML pipelines, and quantum circuit design simultaneously.

TangleLab is addressing this by functioning as an open educational resource, offering hands-on access, workshops, training, and consulting for researchers and students. For forward-thinking IT leaders, the takeaway is clear: the time to build a quantum-ready workforce is now. Organizations that begin upskilling their data scientists and infrastructure architects on hybrid frameworks today will be positioned to seize a definitive competitive advantage as quantum hardware matures.

3 key takeaways for enterprise tech leaders

  1. Quantum is an accelerator, not a replacement: Do not wait for a standalone quantum savior. The future of enterprise compute is hybrid, requiring orchestrations between CPUs, GPUs, and QPUs working together on complex workflows.
  2. Focus on practical utility over theoretical supremacy: Look for immediate areas where “quantum utility” can optimize existing business processes—such as logistics optimization, molecular simulation, or financial risk modeling.
  3. The workforce must be upskilled today: The transition to quantum-classical computing is as much a human talent challenge as a hardware one. Enterprise IT leaders should proactively build pipelines and training programs around hybrid computing concepts.

Listen to the full episode

To dive deeper into how the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center is pioneering the integration of quantum technologies into the modern supercomputing environment, listen to the complete discussion with Dr. Bruno Abreu on This Week in HPC Episode 404: Quantum at PSC on SoundCloud.

The Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center (PSC) actively incorporates AMD architecture across its HPC platforms. Bridges-3, is slated to be built by HPE and will leverage high-core-count AMD EPYC™ CPU nodes for massive parallel processing. The center operates an AMD Heterogeneous Accelerated Compute Cluster (HACC), which features dual AMD EPYC 9654 96-core processors paired with 16 AMD Instinct™ MI210 GPUs and 8 AMD Alveo™ V80 compute accelerator cards. Bridges-2, relies on HPE Cray architecture, deploying AMD EPYC 7742 64-core processors (128 cores per node) across its primary computing resources. Learn more at https://www.psc.edu/. 

*************

HPE and AMD are partnering to deliver the next generation of AI and supercomputing infrastructure. Combining HPE’s deep expertise in large-scale system design with AMD EPYC™ processors and AMD Instinct™ accelerators, the two companies help customers build platforms capable of supporting the most demanding AI, modeling, simulation, and analytics workloads. Whether accelerating scientific research, enabling digital engineering, or training advanced AI models, HPE and AMD focus on what matters most: faster insights, greater efficiency, and the flexibility to scale. Together, they provide the technology foundation organizations need to solve complex problems, drive discovery, and create lasting business and societal impact.

item.title: The new geopolitics of IT: Why sovereign AI is the next boardroom mandate
item.description:
Artificial intelligence has transitioned into a major instrument of corporate strategy and national competitiveness. Driven by a post-pandemic push for digital independence, escalating national security concerns, and multi-billion-dollar government subsidies globally, organizations are rewriting their infrastructure playbooks.

For CIOs and enterprise technology leaders, this “de-globalization” of IT is not just an abstract political trend. It is an immediate operational reality that directly dictates cross-border data governance, supply chain resilience, and the long-term viability of heavy enterprise IT infrastructure investments. As macroeconomic pressures mount, establishing a cohesive digital sovereignty plan has evolved from a conceptual luxury into an essential mandate for the modern boardroom.

The core drivers reshaping enterprise AI strategy

The rapid, grassroots adoption of generative AI across global enterprises has exposed vulnerabilities regarding data privacy, regulatory compliance, and market concentration. When evaluating your organization’s long-term reliance on external AI platforms, three primary catalysts demand immediate attention:

1. The looming threat of cross-border data breaches

Data security remains a primary catalyst for sovereign infrastructure deployment. Enterprise technology leaders face a widening gap where rapid employee adoption of AI tools has outpaced corporate data governance. When internal teams feed proprietary code, strategic plans, or customer data into external public models, that data frequently crosses international boundaries, exposing the enterprise to potential legal and security risks.

The analytical stakes are clear: Gartner predicts that by 2027, more than 40% of AI-related data breaches will result from the improper use of generative AI across geographic borders. Sovereign AI addresses this vulnerability at the architectural level by bounding data within physical geographic borders, helping ensure that sensitive information remains subject to local governance and protected from unauthorized international exposure.

2. Mitigating monopolistic vendor lock-in

In the early stages of the generative AI boom, many organizations rushed to deploy workloads on a handful of hyper-scale cloud providers. However, relying on a highly concentrated market leaves enterprises vulnerable to rigid, proprietary architectures, sudden service disruptions, and monopolistic pricing structures.

If your core operational models are bound to a single provider’s ecosystem, your ability to pivot as the market evolves can be severely restricted. Forward-thinking CIOs are shifting toward sovereign models to reclaim control over their technology stacks, aiming to retain the agility to run workloads where they are most cost-effective and secure.

3. Preserving cultural, regional, and corporate context

Standard commercial AI models rely heavily on English-centric, Western-biased training data. For global enterprises and regional governments, these generic models can lack the nuanced understanding of local languages, regional compliance variations, and unique cultural contexts.

Developing localized corporate or region-specific models helps ensure that unique economic assets, proprietary corporate knowledge, and specific regional contexts are fully preserved and maximized, delivering a distinct competitive edge that generic public models may not replicate.

The hard truth: The operational challenges of “going local”

While the strategic benefits of sovereign AI are clear, executing an independent AI strategy can introduce technical and fiscal hurdles. Designing and maintaining local AI infrastructure requires a level of architectural precision that goes far beyond standard enterprise IT operations.

  • Technical complexity: Setting up standard database servers or enterprise applications follows a well-mapped trajectory. In contrast, designing, optimizing, and deploying high-performance computing (HPC) environments capable of large-scale AI model training is incredibly complex. Every sovereign system requires meticulous custom fine-tuning across computing layers, high-speed networking fabrics, and dense storage arrays to avoid severe performance bottlenecks.
  • Ballooning infrastructure costs: Building and training a proprietary large language model from scratch demands substantial capital. The combined cost of hyper-specialized engineering talent, high-density data center energy requirements, and advanced hardware can quickly push project costs past the $1 billion mark. To make sovereign AI financially viable, technology leaders must focus on sourcing highly cost-effective, energy-efficient underlying hardware paired with open-source software stacks.
  • Navigating evolving international regulation: Public and internal enterprise trust in generative AI remains fragile due to model hallucinations and latent bias. Furthermore, compliance is a moving target. Comprehensive frameworks like the EU AI Act are fundamentally altering the regulatory landscape. Organizations that construct AI infrastructure without deep consideration for future international governance structures risk spending millions to build non-compliant systems that cannot be legally operated.

The strategic solution: The open ecosystem approach

To overcome these technical and fiscal barriers, enterprise technology leaders cannot rely on proprietary systems controlled by a single vendor. Practical sovereignty demands a collaborative, open architecture built on transparent, highly efficient technology. Leading research institutions and enterprise clusters are already demonstrating that sovereign AI can be successfully deployed at scale by utilizing an open ecosystem approach.

Real-world proof points in open infrastructure

Modern, sovereign architectures avoid vendor lock-in while balancing immense workload requirements with practical cost management. Two prominent organizations leading this charge include:

  • The University of Stuttgart (Germany): To drive sovereign model training and high-performance simulation while adhering to European data laws, the university is building its next-generation “Herder” supercomputer. This system leverages the open HPE Cray GX5000 platform alongside AMD Instinct™ GPUs and AMD EPYC™ processors, demonstrating how open-architecture hardware can deliver massive scale without proprietary restrictions.
  • Oak Ridge National Laboratory (United States): This premier research facility is deploying its exascale “Discovery” system and “Lux” AI cluster. These systems provide dedicated sovereign AI factory capabilities for advanced, data-sensitive scientific research, relying on high-density silicon and robust hardware manufacturing to maintain control over their data destiny.

By combining high-density, energy-efficient silicon from AMD with the exascale expertise of HPE, these architectures demonstrate how organizations can mitigate the massive financial and power strains associated with frontier AI workloads.

Actionable next steps for CIOs

Gartner forecasts that 35% of countries will be locked into region-specific AI platforms utilizing proprietary contextual data by 2027. As geographic boundaries increasingly dictate digital capabilities, waiting to define your sovereignty strategy is no longer a viable option.

To secure your enterprise’s digital future, you can act pragmatically today:

  • Map your workloads: Conduct a comprehensive audit to identify where your current AI workloads sit and determine which operations rely on external, third-party systems.
  • Audit cross-border exposure: Assess your data pipeline to identify hidden instances where proprietary corporate data or customer information is crossing geographic borders.
  • Evaluate open alternatives: Explore how an open-architecture foundation combining energy-efficient hardware and open-source software can provide a secure, predictable, and financially sustainable runway for your enterprise’s AI initiatives.

Navigating the intersection of geopolitics, infrastructure complexity, and data governance requires an actionable plan. For more information, The Complexity of Sovereign AI.

item.title: How CIOs can overcome the AI trust gap
item.description:
If you’re like most CIOs, your CEO’s viewpoint of and strategic outlook for AI has likely shifted several times over the past two-plus short years, perhaps even in contradictory ways. Initial doubts or disregard may have given way to full-out FOMO. Demands for copilots everywhere in everyone’s hands may have experienced pullback as the bills and questions of value mounted. Rampant experimentation turned to targeted use cases. Pressure for widespread AI adoption narrowing as “tokenmaxxing” and “tokenomics” entered the lexicon.

Now, with frontier labs showing what can go wrong with “agent misalignment,” AI failures hitting the news, and questions of liability still lingering, trust in AI — and their CIO’s AI strategy — is becoming a key CEO concern (once again).

As the executive setting the company’s course for AI, the CIO is expected to make every AI project pay off, to instill trust in AI for all stakeholders, and to guarantee that nothing unforeseen and unfortunate happens. As a result, the stakes are high, with CIOs already blamed for any AI misstep and, according to IDC, at risk of future firings as lawsuits, fines, and AI incidents rise through 2030.

The only way for CIOs to meet this moment is to establish governance, security, data quality, AI model quality standards, and metrics for business ROI, with a clearcut means of shutting systems down if systems become a risk.

Doing this will take time and money at a time when CEOs are being pressed to show results from AI. It will also require clear and compelling explanations of why all these steps are necessary, how these steps fit into a total corporate AI strategy, what checkpoints can be set to assure that business metrics and investment return goals are met, and how AI should be addressed in the corporate risk management plan.

Here are the essential steps CIOs should take to build trust in their companies’ AI implementations.

1. Require quality data, quality AI models, and business-relevant metrics before projects are launched

To date, many organizations have run their AI projects in “sandbox” mode. They try out different AI models and algorithms, without paying as much attention to the data and the metrics. Here, the most quoted evidence is from MIT’s 2025 AI survey, which found that enterprises had invested nearly $40 billion for generative AI, with 95% of those projects reported as yielding no return.

This year, AI’s honeymoon period has shown signs of being over. CEOs are expecting not only results but returns on their investments. This will only grow louder in 2027. And the only way to get results is to ensure that AI projects use high-quality data, that AI models are developed and maintained to the highest quality, and that clear metrics for investment return that tie to specific business use cases and outcomes are in place.

CIOs must preemptively take the lead in setting AI culture and work standards. Only from that position can trust follow.

2. Run tight, controllable projects

Recent incidents involving OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have shown what can go wrong when AI goes rogue. No enterprise CIO wants this to happen on their watch.

To avoid this, AI projects should be structured with domains of knowledge and functions limited to the environments that they operate in (e.g., support for a call center). These AI projects should not try to do too much at first. As confidence is gained with the AI and its results, scope can be expanded.

A slow, proof-based approach to agentic AI will be essential to ensuring stakeholder trust.

3. Have an AI shut down valve

If an AI project goes awry, do you have a way to shut it down and mitigate any damage?

How to turn an AI system off should be one of the first tasks defined in any AI project plan. It’s equally important to take this one step further — by incorporating shutdown and restoration steps for every AI system in the enterprise. This can be done by including AI in corporate disaster recovery and risk management plans.

For a more granular look, see our partner publication CSO’s “Why you need a reliable AI agent kill switch” and “Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices.”

4. Consider engaging an auditor to monitor AI security, governance, and compliance

There will always be corporate functions — sales, marketing, engineering — that will want to skip governance and get to running AI systems. In companies that stress R&D, there might even be some resistance from the board and CEO, who want to avoid “red tape” and slowdowns.

Regardless of company culture, it will be up to the CIO to advocate for system security, compliance, and governance to ensure AI safety and risk management. CIOs can get around this quandary by hiring an outside audit firm to monitor AI systems for security, governance, and compliance, regularly reporting to the board and citing any irregularities that must be corrected.

5. Pick the right vendors

Vendors offering AI systems or services must have the same level of commitment to quality AI that your company does. AI vendors should be vetted not only for their products and the data that they use, but for the strength of their support, security, governance, compliance, and ability to recover from a disaster.

CSO has more on what IT leaders should consider here, from an AI security vendor lens: See “Key questions CISOs must ask before adopting AI-enabled cyber solutions.”

A final wrap

Harris/Dataiku surveyed 900 CEOs earlier this year, and 80% said their role was at risk if they didn’t deliver AI results by the end of 2026. Moreover, 57% believed that “insufficient AI explainability could trigger a customer trust or brand credibility crisis.”

Trust in AI has become a major issue for CEOs and their boards. Ensuring AI trust should be at the top of CIO AI to-do lists.

item.title: State of IT jobs: AI boosts salaries but also burnout and the gender gap
item.description:
Following the IT and tech hiring boom during the Covid-19 pandemic, companies made space for AI initiatives that resulted in increased layoffs. But new data reveals that some IT hiring trends are starting to turn around.

Pay in the most AI-exposed occupations grew around 46% since 2021, compared to only 25% for jobs in the least-exposed category, according to the Dice Tech Sentiment report. The data reveals this gap began to grow in 2024 and continues to grow as job postings rebound after several rough hiring years.

As organizations begin to realize AI initiatives and investments, they’re now looking to fill their ranks with specialized skillsets, and it’s driving increased compensation. AI has changed the skills businesses need, and 84% of executives report they currently struggle to find specialized local talent while 64% say they feel unprepared for ongoing disruption, according to data from a 2026 report from Globalization Partners.

In a few short years, AI has caused multiple swings in tech hiring. As organizations understand the skills they need to realize AI visions, hiring, for now, appears to be on the upswing for candidates and jobseekers, with more competitive offers. On the employee side, as AI transforms job roles and business functions across every industry, there are, however, increased reports of burnout and a widening gender gap.

Salary boost for specialized skills

AI is currently creating some of the fastest growing and highest paying opportunities in today’s labor market, according to LinkedIn Research. Data reveals that AI job postings have doubled in 2026 from 2023, with the average job listing around $177k in compensation for AI roles, compared to $80k for non-AI roles.

Salary offers and benefit packages have again become more competitive, with 72% of employers saying they’re increasing compensation budgets to attract and retain top talent. Additionally, 65% of tech leaders said they’re offering salaries above their planned range, with 87% stating the top reason being a need to secure candidates with specialized skills, according to Robert Half.

Tech leaders are also seeking specific skills, with 92% acknowledging internal plans to offer higher pay for relevant AI skills. Across every industry, 42% of all business leaders say they’ll pay more for AI-related experience compared to other general tech skills.

Additionally, pay transparency, once relatively taboo in the hiring process, has now become normalized in hiring with 96% of organizations reporting they either already share compensation or plan to soon. Sharing compensation on job postings has several benefits including improving the quality of the candidate pool, more efficient salary negotiation, and a reduced time to hire. Business leaders seem to recognize the benefits, with 67% of employers saying their company takes pay transparency beyond legal requirements, offering more information than is legally required, adds Robert Half.

AI accelerates employee burnout

As daily AI use quadrupled over the past year, burnout doubled and confidence in tech’s long-term future dropped from 80 to 60%, according to Dice. The data reveals around 74% of employees say they plan to change employers in the next year, and 55% say they’re actively job searching, despite only 41% saying they believe they’ll find a better position.

Dice also reveals nearly half of all employed tech professionals report feeling burnout, with around 25% describing themselves as very burned out. And among those reporting burnout, tech and AI professionals express the highest rates.

High levels of burnout can cost companies lost productivity and hurt bottom lines. In 2025, a staggering 10 trillion was estimated to have been lost globally due to disengaged and burnt out employees, according to Globalization Parters. If companies are losing profits through employee burnout, costs of AI investments need to be greater priorities when planning AI initiatives.

AI is meant to boost productivity and efficiency, but Dice says that while speed without guardrails might create advantages for some, it’ll create anxiety for others. Similar to pay transparency, organizations must practice AI transparency. Yet fewer than half of employers report having formal AI policies in place to govern or dictate its use in the enterprise, adds Dice. 

AI gender gap emerges

While there’ve been efforts to move the needle on gender diversity in IT and tech over the years, AI has revealed another gender bias the tech industry will need to contend with to reach gender parity. Tech has always struggled with gender equity despite concerted efforts to make IT and STEM jobs more appealing to women.

Unfortunately, despite efforts to create cultural shifts, AI has once again widened the gender gap in tech. According to further data from LinkedIn Research, women only accounted for 26% of AI hires in the US in 2025, compared to 50% of hires into non-AI roles. And of course, the numbers drop more at the C-suite level, where only 13% of AI leadership at AI companies is held by women.

AI roles have also largely gone to candidates with college degrees with 91% of AI workers holding a bachelor’s degree or higher, moving up to 95% for C-suite and director level positions, so there’s an additional lack of opportunity for those women without a traditional education. Tech and IT leaders will need to avoid falling back into the old hiring patterns that initially caused an absence of representation in tech.

Plus, there’s an emerging gender gap on AI sentiment, with women holding more negative views than their male peers when asked about the impact of AI over the next 20 years, according to data from Pew Research. Women were more likely to say they felt negatively about the impact of AI on themselves personally (33%) and on society overall (43%), compared to 27% and 36% of men who said the same, respectively. Inversely, only 11% of women said they felt positively about AI’s impact on society, while 22% of men said they felt positive.

Women are also more likely to say AI is advancing too quickly — 68% compared to 58% of men. These opposing sentiments might contribute to the overall gender gap in AI roles, as women show more hesitation and caution with AI tools compared to male colleagues.

item.title: The next digital twin isn’t of a machine, it’s of your business
item.description:
The digital twin concept earned its credibility in engineering. Its origins trace to a 2002 University of Michigan presentation in which Michael Grieves described a “Mirrored Spaces Model”: a virtual system holding the information about a physical one, linked to it throughout its life.

For example, a jet engine manufacturer builds a precise virtual replica of a physical turbine, feeds it real-time sensor data, and runs simulations that predict failure before it occurs, optimize maintenance intervals, and test design modifications without touching the physical asset. This model is invaluable because the cost of being wrong about a turbine is high, the variables are measurable, and the physics are well understood. Organizations have applied the same principle to factory floors, supply chains and urban infrastructure, each time with the same underlying logic: a dynamic model of a complex system allows continuous optimization that periodic review cannot match.

However, the enterprise itself has received only part of that treatment. Even Gartner now evaluates organizational digital twin platforms as a category, describing them as dynamic models of how an organization operationalizes its business model, deploys resources and delivers customer value. Yet most of these twins model how work flows, not what it is worth, and that gap is consequential.

A dynamic model of the enterprise

Still, most large organizations still navigate strategic decisions with a picture of themselves that is static, incomplete and economically unattributed. Org charts describe reporting relationships as they were drawn at the last reorganization rather than how people actually interact. Process maps describe intended or designed workflows, not actual ones. And planning documents describe resource allocations as they existed at the time of the last budget cycle. None of these artifacts answer the question that matters most for strategic decision-making: what is the work actually worth, at the level of granularity required to improve it?

A living model of the enterprise changes what is possible. Imagine a representation of how work actually flows across functions (not as designed or conceived, but as executed), where decisions accumulate and slow, where handoffs lose information, where risk concentrates until it surfaces as an incident, and where resources are applied to activities whose economic contribution has never been examined. Connected to real-time operational data, that model moves leaders beyond the static artifacts that currently substitute for organizational self-knowledge.

But a model of how work flows is useful only for operational diagnosis, not a complete economic understanding. Strategic redesign requires knowing what the work measurably produces at the level of individual activities, decision points and handoffs.

Enriching the digital twin with economic process modeling

As I have discussed in previous pieces, Economic Process Modeling (EPM) provides that additional layer. By decomposing processes into their constituent components and attributing value across five dimensions (revenue contribution, cost and friction, risk exposure, option value and information value), EPM transforms a process map from a descriptive artifact into an economic instrument.

The output is not a flowchart but a value ledger: which components are value drags that cost more than they contribute, which are misaligned (a person doing a system’s job, or the reverse), and where value is created but never collected, usually as data the process discards. That is the side of the business case that cost accounting alone cannot show. It is the value layer the enterprise digital twin needs to support strategic decisions rather than merely operational ones.

Douglas Laney

Enterprise, know thyself

The practical benefits of an enterprise digital twin featuring EPM are compound:

  • It enables businesses to model the P&L consequences of a restructuring before headcount decisions are made.
  • It surfaces the process components where AI investments could generate the highest return per dollar–rather than requiring that prioritization to be resolved through stakeholder negotiation and executive sponsorship, which is how it is currently resolved in most organizations.
  • It makes visible the information assets being generated and destroyed by current process designs.
  • And it shows where risk is concentrating in operational workflows before that concentration produces a regulatory finding or a customer failure.

These are not incremental improvements to existing planning processes; they represent a different quality of organizational self-knowledge.

What makes this achievable rather than speculative is that the required inputs exist in most large organizations already. Process mining tools extract actual workflow patterns from system logs, ERP and CRM systems hold the operational and customer data needed to attribute revenue and cost at component level, and risk systems hold the exposure data.

The missing element is the economic model that sits above the infrastructure, translates operational patterns into value attributions, and makes the enterprise legible as an economic system rather than a collection of functions.

Economic process modeling in action

CentrePort, is the port and logistics operator in Wellington, New Zealand. Its CentreConnect freight service generated a high volume of small inter-port charges, each reviewed and reconciled by hand by a small commercial team working from spreadsheets. Rather than automating first, the company modeled the invoicing workflow down to individual container movements, linked each activity to time and cost data, and tested standardization and automation scenarios before committing to change.

Processing time per invoice fell from 25 minutes to 23 seconds. But the more telling outcomes were those a throughput metric would miss: fewer financial discrepancies and less overpayment risk, stronger data governance than spreadsheets allowed, and groundwork for scaling volumes without adding staff. Those are risk, information and option value, not only cost.

CentrePort has since applied the approach to other commercial processes and now treats it as a precondition for change. “Before undertaking any projects, we now ensure that the current state is understood, along with the upstream and downstream impacts of change,” said Tanya Dednam, Head of Digital.

The evolution from physical to enterprise digital twins

As many businesses and the global economy continue to shift toward digital, AI-based and services-oriented offerings, economically modeling the enterprise can become more important than modeling physical things.

However, the analogy to physical digital twins carries an important limitation: Turbine physics are stable whereas organizational economics are contested, context-dependent and subject to strategic choice. An enterprise digital twin built on EPM does not produce a single authoritative answer about what a process component is worth. It produces a structured basis for the argument, with explicit assumptions that can be examined, challenged and revised as conditions change, which is precisely what distinguishes a useful analytical framework from the static planning artifacts it replaces.

The competitive advantage this capability confers is not in the model itself. Rather, it is in the organizational discipline of making economic attribution a continuous practice, of treating the enterprise as an asset to be actively managed rather than a structure to be periodically reorganized when the last reorganization stops working. And rather than an enterprise-wide focus, the practical aperture is a single process with high economic exposure–ideally one already under transformation or AI investment pressure, modeled well enough to inform a real decision or action.

Organizations that model, measure and analyze the EPM-enhanced digital twin of their processes will be able to adapt, optimize and transform with significantly greater agility than those navigating with onerous org charts and planning PowerPoints.

item.title: Microsoft Retires Azure Deployment Environments with No Replacement Product
item.description:
Azure Deployment Environments retires on February 22, 2027 and Microsoft names no successor, telling teams to use Bicep or ARM templates directly. Microsoft Dev Box follows on September 18, 2028, pointed at Windows 365, which Microsoft says is not a one-to-one replacement. Remaining Dev Box workloads should expect deletion.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

item.title: Scaling agentic AI with confidence
item.description:
Your AI agents are making decisions faster than your teams can review them. Governance requires the same speed.

In order to accomplish their given tasks, agents gain access to new applications and business data around the clock. But every autonomous decision raises a question you’ll eventually have to answer: Can you prove the agent acted within policy?

More than half of enterprises are already deploying agentic AI, according to research by Omdia. This growing reliance on AI agents is creating a trust deficit that makes governance and accountability an immediate CIO priority.

Identity governance can help close that deficit by giving CIOs the evidence to demonstrate effective oversight as they expand their use of AI agents.

“Boards are asking CIOs a simple question: can we trust what our AI is doing? Most can’t answer it yet,” said Neil McGlennon, Global Field CTO at SailPoint. “AI has moved from experiment to execution, and closing the trust deficit means knowing which agents exist, what they can access, and who is accountable when they act. Without that, AI stalls at the pilot stage.”

What is audit-ready context?
Boards and auditors expect CIOs to provide clear evidence to back AI agent decisions. This requires context, such as the agent’s identity and human owner, as well as any applications and data involved. The record should also show which policies governed the decision.

This creates a clear line of accountability from the agent’s action back to the person responsible for it. Context needs to be easy to access and understand for non-technical stakeholders.

The case for continuous governance

AI agents rely on a growing number of non-human identities (NHIs) to authenticate and access enterprise resources. These NHIs include machine accounts, API keys, and tokens. Some enterprises have up to 140 NHIs for every employee.

AI agents can quickly change responsibilities and end up retaining permissions they no longer need. This creates unnecessary risk. For example, an agent could keep broad database access after moving from data migration to basic reporting, or keep administrator privileges long after completing a task that required them.

This privilege drift shows why continuous governance matters. Periodic access reviews leave too much time between checks for agents making decisions in real time. Continuous oversight can detect changes in agent behavior and trigger an immediate response, including shutting down an agent when necessary.

The essentials of AI identity governance

Identity and access management (IAM) teams now have AI agents to govern alongside human users. Supporting agentic AI requires three connected capabilities:

  • Discovery and unified visibility
  • Real-time governance and audit
  • Proactive protection and response

Organizations need visibility into the agents and NHIs operating across the enterprise. Governance provides the controls and evidence to oversee their activity, and real-time protection helps teams detect problems and respond immediately.

Keeping AI accountable

AI agents will continue to take on more responsibility across the enterprise, increasing the need for strong identity governance. With the right oversight, CIOs can support broader AI adoption while maintaining accountability for how agents act and what they gain access to.


Explore how CIOs can close the AI trust deficit as agentic AI adoption grows.

item.title: The AI trust deficit: Why explainability, not more automation, is the CIO’s next priority
item.description:
An AI trust deficit occurs when an organization deploys autonomous AI agents faster than it can prove those agents are acting within policy. It’s the gap between what AI agents are doing and what CIOs can clearly explain to a board, auditor, or regulator. Closing that gap requires audit-ready context: evidence showing who owns an agent, what it can access, and which policies governed its decisions.

This gap is widening quickly. More than half of enterprises are already deploying agentic AI, according to Omdia research, and these agents now onboard applications, resolve access requests, and act on business data around the clock. The question is no longer whether AI can move fast. It’s whether you can prove, at any moment, that it moved correctly.

Why the AI trust deficit is a board-level problem

Enterprises want the speed and efficiency that autonomous AI delivers, but speed without accountability creates exposure. When an AI agent makes a decision that no one can trace back to a policy or a person, you don’t have a governance program. You have a liability waiting to surface during your next audit.

The scale of non-human identity has made the issue more urgent. Some enterprises now manage roughly 45 machine identities for every employee, and 67% of enterprise leaders say they’re concerned about the security risk those identities pose. AI agents rely on this same population of API keys, tokens, and service accounts to authenticate and act, which means every new agent amplifies an already sprawling attack surface.

“AI innovation has outpaced AI safety,” says Mike Kiser, director of Strategy and Standards at SailPoint. “The more this gap stretches, the more likely it is that organizations become ticking time bombs just waiting for an incident to happen.”

What audit-ready context actually looks like

Audit-ready context means every AI-driven decision comes with a traceable record, not a black-box outcome. Boards and regulators increasingly expect CIOs to explain not just what an agent did, but why it did it and who is accountable for it.

A defensible answer connects three things every time:

  • Ownership: A named human is responsible for every non-human identity, from creation through retirement.
  • Policy rationale: The specific rule or condition that triggered the agent’s action, tied to a clear business need.
  • Risk evidence: A logged risk score, timestamp, and outcome that justified automation or escalation.

Picture a board asking why a finance access agent approved a request. A CIO with audit-ready context can answer immediately: the agent is owned by the director of financial reporting, the decision followed a specific quarterly access policy, and the action was logged and continuously monitored for behavioral drift. That’s the difference between an explanation and a guess.

Why governance has to be continuous, not periodic

AI agents, business processes, and policies continue to evolve, which means governance has to keep pace or it quickly falls behind. An agent built for one task can retain broad privileges long after its role changes, accumulating access it no longer needs.

Consider how quickly this drift happens in practice:

  • An agent provisioned for temporary data migration keeps its original database privileges after being reassigned to simple reporting.
  • A service desk agent granted administrator-level permissions during a training phase continues running with those privileges long after training ends.
  • A low-privilege chatbot is manipulated through indirect prompt injection into triggering a high-privilege agent that executes unauthorized changes at machine speed.

Periodic reviews can’t catch this kind of drift in time. An agent operating between review cycles can take thousands of actions before anyone notices something went wrong. This is why continuous identity governance, validating access and behavior in real time rather than on a quarterly schedule, has become the baseline expectation, not an enhancement.

Building the foundation for trusted AI

Closing the AI trust deficit starts with treating AI agents the same way you’d treat any privileged digital worker: authenticate every action, authorize every decision, and keep a record of both.

This is where adaptive identity earns its place in the conversation. Rather than relying on static permissions, it adjusts access dynamically as an agent’s role, risk profile, or behavior changes, while still generating the audit trail boards expect. Non-human identity governance extends this same discipline to the machine accounts, tokens, and service identities that agents depend on, ensuring that nothing operates outside your visibility.

A unified platform makes this practical at scale. When identity, access, and policy data live in one control plane rather than scattered across disconnected tools, you can trace a single decision from the moment an agent requests access to the moment that access is approved, denied, or revoked, without stitching together logs from multiple systems after the fact.

Get ahead of the questions your board will ask

Your board and auditors will eventually ask how you’re governing AI, who’s accountable for it, and what evidence proves your safeguards are working. The organizations that answer confidently are the ones that built audit-ready context into their identity program before they needed it.

Download “Closing the AI trust deficit” to learn what explainable AI governance requires and how to build the evidence trail your board will expect.

Then put that knowledge to work with “The CIO agentic AI governance checklist,” a practical two-page assessment for identifying gaps in your AI governance readiness before they become audit findings.
